“That must have been the very period of Mr. Elliot's life,” Anne said, “that has always particularly intrigued me. It must have been around the time he became acquainted with my father and sister. I never knew him then, only heard about him. But something in his behavior towards them, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, has always been difficult to reconcile with the man he is now. It seemed to suggest a different kind of person.”

“I know all about it!” Mrs. Smith exclaimed. “He had met Sir Walter and your sister before I knew him, but he talked about them constantly. I know they invited and encouraged him, and I know he chose not to visit. Perhaps I can explain things you would never expect me to know. As for his marriage, I knew everything at the time. I heard every argument for and against it. I was the friend he trusted with his hopes and plans. Although I hadn't known his wife beforehand—her lower social position would have made that impossible—I knew her throughout the rest of her life, or at least until its last two years. I can answer any question you might want to ask.”

“No,” Anne said, “I have no particular questions about her. I've always understood that they weren't happily married. But I would like to know why, at that stage of his life, he treated my father's friendship so dismissively. My father certainly wanted to show him kind and appropriate attention. Why did Mr. Elliot withdraw?”

“At that time,” Mrs. Smith replied, “Mr. Elliot had one ambition: to make his fortune, and to make it rather faster than a legal career would allow. He had decided to gain it through marriage. At the very least, he was determined not to spoil his prospects with an imprudent marriage. I know he believed—rightly or wrongly, I can't judge—that your father and sister's invitations and courtesies were meant to arrange a match between the heir and the young lady. Such a marriage could not possibly satisfy his ideas of wealth and independence. I assure you, that was why he drew back. He told me the entire story and kept nothing from me. It was curious that, having only just left you behind in Bath, I should find your cousin becoming my first and closest acquaintance after my marriage. Through him, I was continually hearing about your father and sister.

The woman was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed to retain at Lady Canterville's earnest request. As they stepped down, she gave each of them a deep curtsy and said in a quaintly old-fashioned manner, “I welcome you to Canterville Chase.” They followed her through the splendid Tudor hall into the library, a long, low room paneled in black oak, with a large stained-glass window at the far end. Tea had been set out for them. After removing their outdoor wraps, they sat down and looked around while Mrs. Umney attended to them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor beside the fireplace. Entirely unaware of its significance, she said, “I'm afraid something has been spilled there.”

“Yes, madam,” the old housekeeper replied softly. “Blood was spilled on that spot.”

“How horrible!” Mrs. Otis exclaimed. “I don't care for bloodstains in a sitting room at all. It must be removed immediately.”

The old woman smiled and answered in the same low, mysterious voice. “It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, murdered on that very spot by her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon outlived her by nine years, then abruptly disappeared under deeply mysterious circumstances. His body has never been found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. Tourists and other visitors have admired the bloodstain greatly. It cannot be removed.”

“Complete nonsense!” Washington Otis cried. “Pinkerton's Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clear it up in no time.” Before the terrified housekeeper could intervene, he was on his knees, vigorously scrubbing the floor with a small stick that resembled a black cosmetic. Within moments, not a trace of the bloodstain remained.

“I knew Pinkerton would do it!” he announced triumphantly, looking around at his admiring family. He had hardly spoken when a dreadful flash of lightning illuminated the gloomy room, a tremendous thunderclap sent everyone jumping to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What an appalling climate!” the American Minister observed calmly, lighting a long cheroot. “I suppose the old country is so overcrowded that there isn't enough decent weather to go around. I've always maintained that emigration is England's only solution.”

“My dear Hiram,” Mrs. Otis cried, “what can we do with a woman who faints?”

“Charge her for it, like broken dishes,” the Minister replied. “That'll stop her fainting.” And within a few moments, Mrs. Umney did indeed revive.

In a certain town, whose name I shall prudently withhold for several reasons, without supplying an invented one, there stands a public building once common to towns both large and small: a workhouse. In that institution for the poor, on a day and date I need not bother to repeat, since they cannot possibly matter to the reader at this point, the little mortal named at the start of this chapter was born.

For a long time after the parish doctor brought him into this world of sorrow and trouble, nobody could be sure the child would survive long enough to receive any name at all. Had he failed to do so, these memoirs would almost certainly never have appeared. If they had, they would have filled only a couple of pages, earning the priceless distinction of being the shortest and most accurate biography in the literature of any age or country.

I do not intend to argue that being born in a workhouse is, in itself, the luckiest or most enviable experience a human being can have. Yet in this particular case, it was the best thing that could possibly have happened to Oliver Twist. The difficulty was persuading Oliver to begin breathing—a tiresome activity, but one that habit has made necessary for a comfortable life. For some time he lay gasping on a small mattress stuffed with loose fibers, caught between this world and the next, with the balance leaning decidedly towards the next. If, during that short interval, Oliver had been surrounded by attentive grandmothers, worried aunts, experienced nurses, and deeply learned doctors, he would undoubtedly have been killed almost at once. Fortunately, only two people were present: a poor old woman made somewhat confused by an unusually generous helping of beer, and a parish doctor paid under contract to attend such cases. Oliver and Nature were therefore left to settle the question between themselves. After a few struggles, Oliver breathed, sneezed, and began announcing to everyone in the workhouse that the parish had gained another mouth to support. He did this by raising as loud a cry as anyone could reasonably expect from a baby boy who had possessed that useful instrument, a voice, for little more than three minutes and a quarter.
